s.u1.title: What counts as work
s.u1.blurb: Standing all day holding a load is exhausting and is not work. The scientific word is narrower than the everyday one.
s.u2.title: Work has a size and a sign
s.u2.blurb: Force times displacement, in joules. And a minus sign when the force is fighting the motion.
s.u3.title: The energy of moving
s.u3.blurb: Anything in motion can do work on something else. How much depends on the mass and very strongly on the speed.
s.u4.title: The energy of position
s.u4.blurb: Energy can be put somewhere and left there: in a height, in a stretched band, in a bent bow.
s.u5.title: Energy is conserved
s.u5.blurb: It changes form and it goes from one thing to another. The total never changes.
s.u6.title: Power
s.u6.blurb: Two people do the same work and one finishes first. Power is the difference between them.
ch10.u1.work:
Kamali spends the day studying for her exams. She reads, draws diagrams, organises her notes and argues about problems with her friends, and by the evening she is worn out. Everyone would say she has worked hard. In science she has done almost no work at all.

Push a huge rock with everything you have and fail to shift it. You will be exhausted, and no work has been done on the rock, because it has not moved.

Stand still for ten minutes with a heavy load on your head. Your arms ache and the load has not gone anywhere. No work.

Two conditions have to hold, together, before a scientist will call it work:

A force must act on the object, and the object must be displaced.

Miss either one and the work is zero. That is a narrower word than the everyday one, and it is narrow on purpose: defined this way, work turns out to be exactly the thing that transfers energy from one object to another, which is what the rest of the chapter is about.

Climbing a staircase is work. Lifting a book onto a shelf is work. Carrying that book along a level corridor at a steady pace is, by this definition, not.
a.ch10-u1-read-1.title: A narrower word than the one you use
ch10.u1.sort.i0.label: A donkey pulling a cart along a road
ch10.u1.sort.i0.why: A force on the cart and the cart moves. Both conditions met.
ch10.u1.sort.i1.label: A man standing still holding a suitcase
ch10.u1.sort.i1.why: Plenty of force and no displacement, so the work is zero however tired he gets.
ch10.u1.sort.i2.label: A girl lifting a bucket of water from a well
ch10.u1.sort.i2.why: She pulls up and the bucket comes up. The force and the movement are in the same direction.
ch10.u1.sort.i3.label: Pushing a parked lorry as hard as you can without moving it
ch10.u1.sort.i3.why: The force is enormous and the displacement is nothing, so the product is nothing.
ch10.u1.sort.i4.label: A windmill lifting water from a well
ch10.u1.sort.i4.why: The wind drives the pump, the water rises. Work is done on the water.
ch10.u1.sort.i5.label: A student reading a chapter for two hours
ch10.u1.sort.i5.why: Hard, tiring and valuable, and there is no force displacing an object, so it is not work in this sense.
ch10.u1.sort.i6.label: A coolie carrying a box along a level platform at a steady walk
ch10.u1.sort.i6.why: The force holding the box up is vertical and the box is going horizontally, so the force does no work on it.
ask.ch10-u1-sort-2.tired.q: If no work is done, why am I so tired?
ask.ch10-u1-sort-2.tired.a:
Because your body is spending energy even when the object is not moving.

Holding a load still takes a constant effort from your muscles, which twitch and relax over and over to keep the position. Each of those tiny movements uses chemical energy from your food, and a lot of it comes out as heat, which is why you get hot as well as tired.

So energy is certainly being spent. None of it is being transferred to the load, and work in this chapter means energy transferred to the object.
a.ch10-u1-sort-2.title: Work, or not work?
a.ch10-u1-sort-2.blurb: Ask the two questions each time. Was there a force, and did the object move?
ch10.u1.quiz.q0.prompt: What two conditions must both hold for work to be done?
ch10.u1.quiz.q0.o0: A force must act, and the object must be displaced
ch10.u1.quiz.q0.f0: Right. Either one alone gives zero work.
ch10.u1.quiz.q0.o1: A force must act, and the person must get tired
ch10.u1.quiz.q0.f1: Tiredness is about the person. Work is about what happened to the object.
ch10.u1.quiz.q0.o2: The object must move, and it must be heavy
ch10.u1.quiz.q0.f2: Mass does not enter the definition at all, and movement alone is not enough.
ch10.u1.quiz.q1.prompt: You push a wall with all your strength for a minute and it does not move. How much work have you done on the wall?
ch10.u1.quiz.q1.f0: Right. No displacement means no work, whatever the force was.
ch10.u1.quiz.q1.o1: A great deal, because the force was large
ch10.u1.quiz.q1.f1: Work is force times displacement, and the displacement here is zero.
ch10.u1.quiz.q1.o2: Some, because you were pushing for a whole minute
ch10.u1.quiz.q1.f2: Time does not appear in the definition of work.
ch10.u1.quiz.q2.prompt: A porter carries a box along a level platform at a steady speed. How much work does he do on the box?
ch10.u1.quiz.q2.o0: None, because the force holding it up is at right angles to the movement
ch10.u1.quiz.q2.f0: Right. Work counts only the displacement in the direction of the force.
ch10.u1.quiz.q2.o1: A lot, because the box moved a long way
ch10.u1.quiz.q2.f1: The box moved horizontally and the force on it is vertical. The two do not meet.
ch10.u1.quiz.q2.o2: A lot, because the box is heavy
ch10.u1.quiz.q2.f2: Mass alone does not make work.
a.ch10-u1-quiz-3.title: When work is done
ch10.u2.formula:
When a constant force F moves an object a distance s in the direction of the force, the work done is

W = F s

The unit is the newton metre, which is given its own name: the joule, written J. One joule is the work done when a force of one newton moves something one metre along the line of the force.

Work has a size and no direction, which makes it easier to handle than force or velocity. It does, though, have a sign.

When the force points the same way as the movement, the work is positive and energy is going into the object. Lift a bag and you do positive work on it.

When the force points against the movement, the work is negative and energy is coming out of the object. Brakes do negative work on a car. Friction does negative work on anything sliding.

And when the force is at right angles to the movement, it does no work at all. This is why the porter's box gets nothing out of being carried along a platform, and why gravity does no work on a satellite going round a circular orbit.
a.ch10-u2-read-1.title: Force times displacement
ch10.u2.calc.c0.prompt: A force of 7 N acts on an object and moves it 8 m in the direction of the force. How much work is done?
ch10.u2.calc.c0.trap: Adding instead of multiplying. Work is a product.
ch10.u2.calc.c1.prompt: A porter lifts a 15 kg suitcase from the ground onto his head, 1.5 m up. How much work does he do on it? Take g as 10 m/s².
ch10.u2.calc.c1.s0: The force needed is the weight: mg, which is 150 N
ch10.u2.calc.c1.trap: Multiplying 15 by 1.5 and answering 22.5. The force is the weight in newtons, not the mass in kilograms.
ch10.u2.calc.c2.prompt: A pair of bullocks exerts a force of 140 N on a plough, and the field is 15 m long. How much work is done in ploughing its length?
ch10.u2.calc.c2.trap: Nothing hidden here. It is worth doing to see what an ordinary day's work comes to in joules.
ch10.u2.calc.c3.prompt: A braking force of 500 N acts on a car while it travels a further 12 m before stopping. How much work does the brake do on the car?
ch10.u2.calc.c3.s0: The force opposes the displacement, so the work is negative
ch10.u2.calc.c3.trap: Giving 6000 and losing the sign. The minus is saying that energy left the car, which is exactly what a brake is for.
a.ch10-u2-calc-2.title: Working out the work
ch10.u2.sort.i0.label: You lift a bag from the floor onto a table
ch10.u2.sort.i0.why: Your force is upwards and the bag goes upwards.
ch10.u2.sort.i1.label: Gravity acts on that bag while you lift it
ch10.u2.sort.i1.why: Gravity pulls down while the bag goes up, so it takes energy out.
ch10.u2.sort.i2.label: Friction acts on a box you are sliding across a floor
ch10.u2.sort.i2.why: Friction always points against the motion, so its work is always negative.
ch10.u2.sort.i3.label: The brakes act on a car that is slowing down
ch10.u2.sort.i3.why: The brake force opposes the movement, which is how the car loses its energy.
ch10.u2.sort.i4.label: Gravity acts on a satellite in a circular orbit
ch10.u2.sort.i4.why: The pull is towards the centre and the satellite moves at right angles to it, so no work is done at all.
ch10.u2.sort.i5.label: You push a crate and it slides forward
ch10.u2.sort.i5.why: Force and displacement in the same direction.
ask.ch10-u2-sort-3.satellite.q: If gravity does no work on a satellite, what keeps it up there?
ask.ch10-u2-sort-3.satellite.a:
Nothing needs to keep it up. It is falling, and missing.

Gravity is certainly acting, and it is certainly changing the satellite's velocity: it turns it, continuously, which is what keeps the path curved into an orbit. What it does not do is change the speed, and work is exactly the thing that changes speed.

The force points at the centre of the earth and the satellite moves at right angles to that, at every instant. A force at right angles to the motion does no work, so the satellite's kinetic energy never changes and it goes round forever.
a.ch10-u2-sort-3.title: Positive, negative or zero?
a.ch10-u2-sort-3.blurb: Compare the direction of the force with the direction the object actually moved.
ch10.u2.quiz.q0.o0: The work done when 1 N moves an object 1 m along the line of the force
ch10.u2.quiz.q0.f0: Right, and it is the unit of energy as well as of work.
ch10.u2.quiz.q0.o1: The force needed to move 1 kg one metre
ch10.u2.quiz.q0.f1: A joule is not a force. The newton is.
ch10.u2.quiz.q0.o2: The energy a 1 kg object has when it is 1 m up
ch10.u2.quiz.q0.f2: That energy happens to be 9.8 J, not 1 J, and it is not the definition.
ch10.u2.quiz.q1.prompt: A ball is thrown upwards. What kind of work does gravity do on it while it rises?
ch10.u2.quiz.q1.f0: Right. Gravity pulls down while the ball goes up, so it takes energy out of the ball.
ch10.u2.quiz.q1.f1: That is what gravity does on the way back down.
ch10.u2.quiz.q1.f2: The force and the movement are along the same line, so work is certainly being done.
ch10.u2.quiz.q2.prompt: An object moves a long way, but the force on it is at right angles to the movement. How much work does that force do?
ch10.u2.quiz.q2.f0: Right. Only displacement in the direction of the force counts.
ch10.u2.quiz.q2.o1: A great deal, because the distance is large
ch10.u2.quiz.q2.f1: The distance in the direction of the force is zero, so the product is zero.
ch10.u2.quiz.q2.o2: Half of what it would do along the line
ch10.u2.quiz.q2.f2: There is no halving rule. A right angle gives exactly nothing.
a.ch10-u2-quiz-4.title: Work, and its sign
ch10.u3.energy:
A fast cricket ball hits a wicket and the wicket is thrown out of the ground. A raised hammer falls on a nail and drives it into the wood. A wound-up toy car is put down and moves off. A pressed balloon springs back, and if you press it hard enough it bursts with a bang.

In every case something was able to exert a force on something else and move it. That capacity is what we call energy. The object that does the work loses energy and the object the work is done on gains it, which is why energy is measured in the same unit as work: the joule.

Energy comes in several forms, and this chapter names five: mechanical energy, which is kinetic plus potential, heat, chemical, electrical and light. The Sun is the source of nearly all of them. Coal and petrol are old sunlight; wind comes from the Sun heating the air unevenly; food comes from plants that used sunlight to make it. A few sources are not from the Sun, including the heat inside the earth and the tides.

A moving object has energy because of its motion, and this is called kinetic energy. A bullet, a flowing river, a falling coconut and a running athlete all have it. It grows with the mass, and it grows very fast indeed with the speed.
a.ch10-u3-read-1.title: Energy is the capacity to do work
ch10.u3.sand.predict.prompt: You drop the same ball into wet sand from 25 cm, then 50 cm, then 1.5 m. What will the three dents look like?
ch10.u3.sand.predict.o0: All three the same, because it is the same ball
ch10.u3.sand.predict.o1: Deeper each time, and the last one much deeper than twice the first
ch10.u3.sand.predict.o2: Deeper each time, in exact proportion to the height
ch10.u3.sand.predict.o3: Shallower from greater heights, because the ball bounces
ch10.u3.sand.observe: Measure each dent with a ruler and write the three depths next to the three heights.
ch10.u3.sand.explain:
The deeper dent means more work was done on the sand, so the ball arrived with more energy.

It arrived faster from a greater height, and kinetic energy goes with the square of the speed. Dropping from six times the height gives a ball travelling about two and a half times as fast, which is about six times the kinetic energy. The depths grow faster than the heights would suggest if you were only counting speed.

This is also the whole reason a fall from a first floor is far more than twice as dangerous as a fall from half that height.
ch10.u3.do.steps:
1. Smooth the sand flat and mark a chalk line on the wall at 25 cm, 50 cm and 1.5 m.
2. Hold the ball at the 25 cm mark and let it fall without pushing it.
3. Lift the ball out carefully and measure the depth of the dent.
4. Smooth the sand and repeat from 50 cm, then from 1.5 m.
5. Write the three heights and the three depths side by side.
6. Six times the height. Is the dent six times as deep? Discuss what else changed.
ch10.u3.do.watch: Someone will push the ball downwards instead of releasing it, which adds energy from the hand and ruins the comparison. Insist on a clean release from a still hand.
a.ch10-u3-do-2.title: Drop a ball into sand
a.ch10-u3-do-2.blurb: The same ball from three heights, into a wet sand bed. Measure the dents.
ch10.u3.calc.c0.prompt: An object of mass 15 kg moves at 4 m/s. What is its kinetic energy?
ch10.u3.calc.c0.trap: Forgetting to square the velocity and answering 30.
ch10.u3.calc.c1.prompt: An object of mass 10 kg moves at 5 m/s. Its speed is then doubled to 10 m/s. What is its kinetic energy now?
ch10.u3.calc.c1.trap: Expecting double. The kinetic energy at 5 m/s was 125 J, and doubling the speed made it four times larger, not twice.
ch10.u3.calc.c2.prompt: A 1500 kg car is travelling at 20 m/s. How much work must be done on it to bring it to rest?
ch10.u3.calc.c2.s0: The work done equals the change in kinetic energy
ch10.u3.calc.c2.s1: Starting Ek is half times 1500 times 400, which is 300,000 J
ch10.u3.calc.c2.s3: So 300,000 J has to be taken out
ch10.u3.calc.c2.trap: Giving a negative answer. The question asks how much work has to be done, which is a size. The brake's own work on the car is minus this.
ch10.u3.calc.c3.prompt: A stone of mass 0.2 kg has a kinetic energy of 10 J. How fast is it moving?
ch10.u3.calc.c3.s0: Ek = half m v squared, so v squared = 2 Ek over m
ch10.u3.calc.c3.trap: Dividing 10 by 0.2 and stopping at 50. The square root is the last step and it is easy to skip.
ask.ch10-u3-calc-3.square.q: Why does the speed get squared and the mass not?
ask.ch10-u3-calc-3.square.a:
Because the speed does its work twice over.

The short argument is the algebra. Work is F times s, F is ma, and the three equations of motion give s = (v squared minus u squared) over 2a. Multiply those together and the a cancels, leaving half m v squared. The v arrived squared from the distance, not from the force.

The practical version is the one to carry around. Double the mass of a car and you double the energy that has to be removed to stop it. Double its speed and you have four times as much to remove. This is why speed limits matter more than vehicle weight, and why the braking distance in chapter 7 went with the square as well.
a.ch10-u3-calc-3.title: Kinetic energy
ch10.u3.quiz.q0.prompt: What is the kinetic energy of an object of mass m moving at velocity v?
ch10.u3.quiz.q0.f0: Right, and its unit is the joule.
ch10.u3.quiz.q0.f1: That is the momentum, which is chapter 8 and a different quantity.
ch10.u3.quiz.q0.f2: That is the potential energy of an object at a height h.
ch10.u3.quiz.q1.prompt: The speed of an object is doubled. What happens to its kinetic energy?
ch10.u3.quiz.q1.f0: Right. The velocity is squared, so doubling it quadruples the energy.
ch10.u3.quiz.q1.f1: That would be true if v were not squared. It is.
ch10.u3.quiz.q1.f2: Kinetic energy depends on the speed, so changing the speed changes it.
ch10.u3.quiz.q2.prompt: A parked lorry and a flying bullet. Which has the greater kinetic energy?
ch10.u3.quiz.q2.f0: Right. A speed of zero makes the whole expression zero, whatever the mass.
ch10.u3.quiz.q2.o1: The lorry, because it is far heavier
ch10.u3.quiz.q2.f1: Multiply by the velocity squared and the lorry's comes to nothing.
ch10.u3.quiz.q2.f2: One of them is zero and the other is not.
a.ch10-u3-quiz-4.title: Kinetic energy
ch10.u4.potential:
Stretch a rubber band and let one end go. It snaps back. While you were stretching it you did work on it, and that work did not make the band move faster: it went into the band's stretched shape and waited there.

Wind the key of a toy car and the same thing happens, this time in a spring. Bend a bamboo bow and the energy goes into the bend, and comes out again as the arrow leaves. Lift an object onto a shelf and the energy goes into its height.

Energy stored because of position or shape is called potential energy. It is the quiet half of mechanical energy: the object is not doing anything with it, and the moment something lets go it will.

For the case of height, the amount is easy to work out. To raise an object of mass m through a height h you have to push up with at least its weight, mg, through a distance h. The work done is mg times h, and all of it ends up stored:

Eₚ = m g h

Two things about that are worth noticing. The height h is measured from somewhere, and you choose where. The same book has one potential energy with respect to the table and a different one with respect to the floor, and neither answer is wrong as long as you say which you meant.

And the path does not matter. Carry a crate straight up a ladder or push it up a long ramp; as long as it ends up at the same height, the work done against gravity is the same mgh.
a.ch10-u4-read-1.title: Energy you can put somewhere and leave
ch10.u4.calc.c0.prompt: An object of mass 10 kg is at a height of 6 m above the ground. What is its potential energy? Take g as 9.8 m/s².
ch10.u4.calc.c0.trap: Leaving out g and answering 60. The 9.8 is what turns kilograms and metres into joules.
ch10.u4.calc.c1.prompt: An object of mass 12 kg has a potential energy of 480 J with respect to the ground. How high is it? Take g as 10 m/s².
ch10.u4.calc.c1.s0: Ep = m g h, so h = Ep over m g
ch10.u4.calc.c1.s1: m g is 12 times 10, which is 120
ch10.u4.calc.c1.trap: Dividing 480 by 12 and answering 40. The g has to come out as well.
ch10.u4.calc.c2.prompt: A crate of mass 40 kg is raised 5 m above the ground. What is its potential energy? Take g as 10 m/s².
ch10.u4.calc.c2.trap: Nothing hidden. The next question uses this answer.
ch10.u4.calc.c3.prompt: That same crate is allowed to fall. What is its kinetic energy when it is halfway down? Take g as 10 m/s².
ch10.u4.calc.c3.g0: It started with 2000 J of potential energy
ch10.u4.calc.c3.g1: Halfway down means h is now 2.5 m
ch10.u4.calc.c3.s0: Potential energy now: 40 times 10 times 2.5, which is 1000 J
ch10.u4.calc.c3.s1: The total has not changed, so the rest must be kinetic
ch10.u4.calc.c3.trap: Thinking the kinetic energy must still be zero because the crate has not landed yet. It has been gaining speed the whole way.
ask.ch10-u4-calc-2.zerolevel.q: If I can choose where to measure the height from, can I make the potential energy whatever I like?
ask.ch10-u4-calc-2.zerolevel.a:
You can choose where zero is, and it changes the number. It never changes anything that happens.

A book on a table has one potential energy measured from the table and a larger one measured from the floor. Both are correct, and you have to say which you meant.

What matters physically is always a difference: how much the energy changed when something moved. Drop the book to the floor and the energy released is mgh with h measured from the table to the floor, whichever level you called zero. The choice cancels out of every real answer, which is why it is safe to make it freely.
a.ch10-u4-calc-2.title: Potential energy
ch10.u4.quiz.q0.prompt: What is the potential energy of an object of mass m raised to a height h?
ch10.u4.quiz.q0.f0: Right, and it equals the work done in raising it against gravity.
ch10.u4.quiz.q0.f1: There is no squared height, and no half.
ch10.u4.quiz.q0.f2: Without g the answer is not in joules at all.
ch10.u4.quiz.q1.prompt: A crate is taken to the top of a building, once straight up by a lift and once up a long ramp. How does the work done against gravity compare?
ch10.u4.quiz.q1.f0: Right. The work against gravity depends only on the change in height.
ch10.u4.quiz.q1.o1: More up the ramp, because it is longer
ch10.u4.quiz.q1.f1: The ramp is longer and gentler, and the two cancel exactly.
ch10.u4.quiz.q1.o2: More in the lift, because it is faster
ch10.u4.quiz.q1.f2: Speed does not change the work. It changes the power, which is a later topic.
ch10.u4.quiz.q2.prompt: A book lies on a table. What is its potential energy?
ch10.u4.quiz.q2.o0: It depends on where you choose to measure the height from
ch10.u4.quiz.q2.f0: Right. With respect to the table it is zero, and with respect to the floor it is not.
ch10.u4.quiz.q2.o1: Zero, because it is not moving
ch10.u4.quiz.q2.f1: Potential energy is about position, not motion. A still object can have plenty.
ch10.u4.quiz.q2.o2: Zero, because it is resting on something
ch10.u4.quiz.q2.f2: Resting on something says nothing about how high that something is.
a.ch10-u4-quiz-3.title: Potential energy
ch10.u5.lab.predict.prompt: An object is dropped from a height. As it falls, what happens to the sum of its potential and kinetic energy?
ch10.u5.lab.predict.o0: It grows, because the object is speeding up
ch10.u5.lab.predict.o1: It shrinks, because the height is being used up
ch10.u5.lab.predict.o2: It stays exactly the same the whole way down
ch10.u5.lab.observe: Run the drop and watch the whole bar, not the two colours inside it.
ch10.u5.lab.explain:
The bar never changes length. One colour shrinks at exactly the rate the other grows.

At the top the object is still, so all of its energy is potential: mgh. At the bottom the height is gone, so all of it is kinetic: half m v squared. In between, every joule that leaves the potential side arrives on the kinetic side.

That is the law of conservation of energy. Energy is not created and not destroyed. It changes form, and the total before and after any change is the same.

Now move the mass slider and run it again. The bar gets longer, because a heavier object starts with more potential energy, and the two halves still trade exactly.
ch10.u5.lab.t1.label: Drop 2 kg from 5 m.
ch10.u5.lab.t1.asks: At the start the bar is all one colour. Which, and why?
ch10.u5.lab.t2.label: Drop 6 kg from the same height.
ch10.u5.lab.t2.asks: The bar is three times as long. Did the object take any longer to fall?
ch10.u5.lab.t3.label: Drop half a kilogram.
ch10.u5.lab.t3.asks: A short bar this time. Say in one sentence what stayed the same across all three runs.
ch10.u5.lab.closing: Potential plus kinetic never changes while an object is falling freely. The two halves trade places and the total stays put.
ask.ch10-u5-lab-1.ground.q: What happens to the energy when the object hits the ground?
ask.ch10-u5-lab-1.ground.a:
It does not disappear. It goes somewhere less convenient.

Most of it becomes heat in the object and in whatever it landed on, both of which are very slightly warmer afterwards. Some of it goes into sound, which is why a landing makes a noise. Some goes into permanently changing the shape of things: a dent in the ground, a crack in the object.

Add all of that up and you get exactly the kinetic energy the object arrived with. The law holds. The reason it looks as though energy has been lost is that heat spread thinly through a floor is useless for doing work, and the forms we can use are the ones we notice.
a.ch10-u5-lab-1.title: One bar, two halves
a.ch10-u5-lab-1.blurb: A 2 kg object dropped from 5 m. The bar underneath is the energy it has, and where that energy currently is.
ch10.u5.pendulum.predict.prompt: You pull a pendulum bob to one side and let it go. Where in its swing is it moving fastest?
ch10.u5.pendulum.predict.o0: At the highest point of the swing
ch10.u5.pendulum.predict.o1: At the lowest point, in the middle
ch10.u5.pendulum.predict.o2: Exactly halfway up on the way back
ch10.u5.pendulum.predict.o3: It moves at the same speed throughout
ch10.u5.pendulum.observe: Watch the bob at the two ends of the swing and at the middle. Mark the middle point with chalk.
ch10.u5.pendulum.explain:
At the two ends the bob is momentarily still, and at those moments all its energy is potential, because it is at its highest. At the bottom it is at its lowest and its fastest, and all of that energy is now kinetic.

Every swing is the same trade, twice over, back and forth.

It does eventually stop, and that is not a failure of the law. Air resistance and friction at the pivot do negative work on it, a little each swing, and that energy becomes heat and sound spread through the air and the string.
ch10.u5.do.steps:
1. Hang the stone on the string so it swings freely without touching anything.
2. Chalk a mark on the floor directly under the resting bob.
3. Pull the bob to one side, note how high it is, and let it go without a push.
4. Watch the two ends of the swing. Note that the bob is still for an instant at each.
5. Note where it is moving fastest.
6. Count the swings until it stops, and discuss where that energy went.
ch10.u5.do.watch: A student who says the bob stops because it runs out of energy. It runs out of usable energy, which has gone into warming the air and the pivot. The distinction is the whole point of the law.
a.ch10-u5-do-2.title: Watch a pendulum trade it back and forth
a.ch10-u5-do-2.blurb: A stone on a string. Where is it fastest, where does it stop, and why does it eventually give up?
ch10.u5.calc.c0.prompt: The object is still at 4 m, just released. What is its potential energy?
ch10.u5.calc.c0.trap: Nothing hidden. This number is the total, and every later row has to add up to it.
ch10.u5.calc.c1.prompt: It has fallen to 3 m. What is its kinetic energy there?
ch10.u5.calc.c1.g1: Potential energy at 3 m: 20 times 10 times 3
ch10.u5.calc.c1.trap: Working out the speed first. It is quicker and safer to subtract, because the total is fixed.
ch10.u5.calc.c2.prompt: It has fallen to 2 m. What is its kinetic energy?
ch10.u5.calc.c2.trap: Halfway down, and the two are now equal. It is worth noticing where that happens.
ch10.u5.calc.c3.prompt: It is just above the ground. What is its kinetic energy?
ch10.u5.calc.c3.g1: Height is now almost zero, so Ep is almost zero
ch10.u5.calc.c3.trap: Thinking some of it has been used up on the way. Nothing was spent. It was moved from one column to the other.
a.ch10-u5-calc-3.title: Filling in the table
a.ch10-u5-calc-3.blurb: A 20 kg object dropped from 4 m, with g taken as 10 m/s². Work out each row and watch the last column.
ch10.u5.quiz.q0.prompt: The potential energy of a freely falling object decreases all the way down. Does that break the law of conservation of energy?
ch10.u5.quiz.q0.o0: No. The kinetic energy grows by exactly as much
ch10.u5.quiz.q0.f0: Right. The sum of the two is the same at every point of the fall.
ch10.u5.quiz.q0.f1: Nothing is lost. One column is emptying into the other.
ch10.u5.quiz.q0.o2: No, because the law applies only to objects at rest
ch10.u5.quiz.q0.f2: The law applies to everything, moving or not.
ch10.u5.quiz.q1.prompt: A pendulum eventually stops swinging. Where did its energy go?
ch10.u5.quiz.q1.o0: Mostly into heat, through air resistance and friction at the pivot
ch10.u5.quiz.q1.f0: Right. The energy is still in the universe, spread so thinly through the air that nothing can use it.
ch10.u5.quiz.q1.f1: Energy cannot be destroyed. Friction moves it into a form you cannot get back.
ch10.u5.quiz.q1.f2: It was there, and it lifted the bob on every swing until it ran out.
ch10.u5.quiz.q2.prompt: Where in a free fall is the kinetic energy largest?
ch10.u5.quiz.q2.o0: Just before it hits the ground
ch10.u5.quiz.q2.f0: Right. The height is nearly gone by then, so nearly all of the energy is kinetic.
ch10.u5.quiz.q2.o1: At the moment it is released
ch10.u5.quiz.q2.f1: At the release it is still, so its kinetic energy is zero.
ch10.u5.quiz.q2.f2: Halfway down the two are equal, so neither is at its largest.
a.ch10-u5-quiz-4.title: Conservation of energy
ch10.u6.power:
Two students of the same weight climb the same rope to the same height. One takes 15 seconds and the other takes 20. They have done exactly the same work, because the work depends only on the weight and the height.

What differs is how fast they did it, and that is power.

P = W / t

The unit is the watt, named after James Watt, and one watt is one joule per second. A thousand watts is a kilowatt, and that is the unit on every appliance in a house.

Power varies from moment to moment, so what is usually quoted is the average power: the total energy used divided by the total time it took.

This is also the unit your electricity bill is written in, although the bill hides it. A bill is in units, and one unit is one kilowatt hour: a kilowatt of power drawn for one hour. That comes to 3,600,000 joules, which is why nobody writes bills in joules.

A more powerful machine does not do more work. It does the same work sooner.
a.ch10-u6-read-1.title: How fast the work gets done
ch10.u6.calc.c0.prompt: A girl of weight 400 N climbs a rope to a height of 8 m in 20 s. What power does she expend?
ch10.u6.calc.c0.s0: Work done is weight times height: 400 times 8, which is 3200 J
ch10.u6.calc.c0.s1: P = W over t, so 3200 divided by 20
ch10.u6.calc.c0.trap: Dividing 400 by 20 and ignoring the height. Power needs the work first.
ch10.u6.calc.c1.prompt: A second girl of the same weight climbs the same 8 m, but takes 50 s. What power does she expend?
ch10.u6.calc.c1.g0: Work done: 3200 J, exactly as before
ch10.u6.calc.c1.trap: Expecting the work to differ too. The work is identical, and only the time is not.
ch10.u6.calc.c2.prompt: A boy of mass 50 kg runs up 45 steps, each 15 cm high, in 9 s. What is his power? Take g as 10 m/s².
ch10.u6.calc.c2.trap: Leaving the step height in centimetres. 15 cm is 0.15 m, and getting that wrong multiplies the answer by a hundred.
ch10.u6.calc.c3.prompt: A household uses 250 units of electricity in a month. How much energy is that in joules?
ch10.u6.calc.c3.g2: 1 kW is 1000 W, and 1 hour is 3600 s
ch10.u6.calc.c3.s0: One kilowatt hour is 1000 times 3600, which is 3,600,000 J
ch10.u6.calc.c3.trap: Multiplying 250 by 1000 and stopping. The hour has to become seconds as well.
ask.ch10-u6-calc-2.unit.q: Why is the electricity bill written in units rather than joules?
ask.ch10-u6-calc-2.unit.a:
Because the joule is far too small for a household.

One unit is 3,600,000 joules. A family using 250 units a month is using nine hundred million joules, and nobody wants a bill with that number on it.

The unit is also honest about what is being sold. The meter is counting kilowatts drawn, multiplied by hours drawn for, which is exactly how the supply company thinks about it. A 1000 W heater left on for one hour costs one unit, and so does a 100 W fan left on for ten hours.
a.ch10-u6-calc-2.title: Power
chal.ch10-u6-challenge-3.goal: A house is using 220 units of electricity a month. One unit is one kilowatt drawn for one hour. Get the month down to 150 units or fewer, and be able to say in each case where the energy was going.
chal.ch10-u6-challenge-3.geyser.label: Run the 2000 W water heater for 15 minutes a day instead of an hour
chal.ch10-u6-challenge-3.geyser.because: 2000 W is 2 kW, so an hour a day is 2 units a day and 60 a month. Three quarters of an hour saved is 45 units.
chal.ch10-u6-challenge-3.geyser.wrong: A water heater is the biggest appliance in the house, so turning it down always saves the most, whatever the hours.
chal.ch10-u6-challenge-3.bulbs.label: Replace ten 60 W bulbs with 9 W LEDs, used 5 hours a day
chal.ch10-u6-challenge-3.bulbs.because: Ten bulbs saving 51 W each is 510 W. Five hours a day for thirty days is 150 hours, and 0.51 kW times 150 is about 77 units. Only a third of the lights run that long, so call it 23.
chal.ch10-u6-challenge-3.bulbs.wrong: An LED is brighter, so it must be using more energy to produce that light.
chal.ch10-u6-challenge-3.fridge.label: Keep the fridge door shut and set it one notch warmer
chal.ch10-u6-challenge-3.fridge.because: A fridge runs its compressor only when it needs to. Less heat getting in means fewer hours of running, and the power is the same while it runs.
chal.ch10-u6-challenge-3.fridge.wrong: A fridge draws the same power all day whatever you do, so the door makes no difference to the bill.
chal.ch10-u6-challenge-3.iron.label: Iron all the week's clothes in one session instead of daily
chal.ch10-u6-challenge-3.iron.because: A 1000 W iron spends several minutes heating up each time it is switched on, and that energy is thrown away when it cools.
chal.ch10-u6-challenge-3.iron.wrong: Ironing more clothes at once makes the iron work harder, so it is the same energy either way.
chal.ch10-u6-challenge-3.standby.label: Switch the television and set-top box off at the wall at night
chal.ch10-u6-challenge-3.standby.because: Standby draws a few watts, which is small, but it runs for every one of the 720 hours in a month.
chal.ch10-u6-challenge-3.standby.wrong: A television on standby draws no power at all, so this saves nothing and is only tidy.
chal.ch10-u6-challenge-3.heater.label: Add a 1500 W room heater for two hours every evening
chal.ch10-u6-challenge-3.heater.because: 1.5 kW for 2 hours is 3 units a day, which is 90 units a month. Heating is expensive because the power is large and the hours are long.
chal.ch10-u6-challenge-3.heater.wrong: A heater only warms the air, so it cannot use much energy.
ch10.u6.challenge.debrief:
Two numbers decide everything on that list: how many watts, and for how many hours. A big appliance used briefly can cost less than a small one left on all month, which is why standby is worth switching off and why the water heater is the first thing to look at.

The arithmetic is the same every time. Watts, divided by a thousand, times hours. That is the unit, and that is the bill.
a.ch10-u6-challenge-3.title: Get the month's bill down
a.ch10-u6-challenge-3.blurb: A household is using 220 units a month and wants to be under 150. Every choice has to be defended.
ch10.u6.quiz.q0.f0: Right, and its unit is the watt, which is one joule per second.
ch10.u6.quiz.q0.f1: That is the work. Power is how fast that work happened.
ch10.u6.quiz.q0.f2: Force is measured in newtons and is a different quantity altogether.
ch10.u6.quiz.q1.prompt: Two people do the same work, one in 10 s and one in 20 s. Compare their work and their power.
ch10.u6.quiz.q1.o0: Same work, and the faster one has twice the power
ch10.u6.quiz.q1.f0: Right. The work depends on the force and the distance, neither of which changed.
ch10.u6.quiz.q1.o1: The faster one did twice the work
ch10.u6.quiz.q1.f1: The work is identical. Only the time differs.
ch10.u6.quiz.q1.f2: Power is work over time, and the times differ by a factor of two.
ch10.u6.quiz.q2.prompt: A lamp uses 1000 J of electrical energy in 10 s. What is its power?
ch10.u6.quiz.q2.f1: That is the energy, not the energy per second.
ch10.u6.quiz.q2.f2: That is the time, not the power.
a.ch10-u6-quiz-4.title: Power
mis.tiredness-means-work.statement: If the effort made you tired, work was done.
mis.tiredness-means-work.correction: Tiredness is about the person. Work is about what happened to the object, and a load held still has had nothing happen to it.
mis.heavy-means-work.statement: Work is done whenever a heavy object is involved.
mis.heavy-means-work.correction: Mass does not appear in the definition. A force and a displacement do.
mis.force-alone-is-work.statement: A large enough force counts as work even if nothing moves.
mis.force-alone-is-work.correction: Work is force times displacement. A displacement of zero makes the product zero however large the force.
mis.time-makes-work.statement: Pushing for long enough counts as work.
mis.time-makes-work.correction: Time does not appear in the definition of work at all. It appears in the definition of power.
mis.any-movement-is-work.statement: Any force and any movement together mean work was done.
mis.any-movement-is-work.correction: Only displacement along the direction of the force counts. A force at right angles to the motion does none.
mis.joule-is-a-force.statement: The joule is a unit of force.
mis.joule-is-a-force.correction: The newton is. A joule is a newton metre: the work done when 1 N moves something 1 m.
mis.joule-is-a-height.statement: A joule is the energy a 1 kg object has at a height of 1 m.
mis.joule-is-a-height.correction: That energy is 9.8 J. A joule is defined from force and distance, not from mass and height.
mis.gravity-always-positive.statement: Gravity always does positive work on an object.
mis.gravity-always-positive.correction: Only while the object is going down. On the way up gravity opposes the motion and does negative work.
mis.gravity-never-works.correction: It does plenty on anything that changes height. It does none only when the motion is at right angles to it.
mis.right-angle-gives-half.statement: A force at right angles to the motion does half its usual work.
mis.right-angle-gives-half.correction: It does exactly none. There is no halving rule.
mis.kinetic-energy-is-momentum.statement: Kinetic energy is mass times velocity.
mis.kinetic-energy-is-momentum.correctio: That is momentum. Kinetic energy is half the mass times the velocity squared, and the two behave very differently.
mis.kinetic-is-potential.statement: Kinetic energy and potential energy are the same quantity.
mis.kinetic-is-potential.correction: One is about motion and the other about position. A still object high up has plenty of the second and none of the first.
mis.energy-follows-speed.statement: Doubling the speed doubles the kinetic energy.
mis.energy-follows-speed.correction: The velocity is squared, so doubling the speed gives four times the energy.
mis.energy-ignores-speed.statement: Kinetic energy depends only on the mass.
mis.energy-ignores-speed.correction: It depends on the speed very strongly indeed, because the speed is squared.
mis.heavier-means-more-energy.statement: The heavier object always has the greater kinetic energy.
mis.heavier-means-more-energy.correction: Not if it is standing still. A speed of zero makes the whole expression zero.
mis.potential-has-a-square.statement: Potential energy is half m h squared.
mis.potential-has-a-square.correction: There is no square and no half. It is m g h, which is the work done lifting it.
mis.potential-leaves-out-g.statement: Potential energy is mass times height.
mis.potential-leaves-out-g.correction: Without g the answer is not in joules. The force you had to apply was the weight, which is mg.
mis.longer-path-more-work.statement: Taking a longer route to the same height means more work against gravity.
mis.longer-path-more-work.correction: The work against gravity depends only on the change in height. A long ramp and a short ladder to the same place cost the same.
mis.faster-means-more-work.statement: Doing something faster means doing more work.
mis.faster-means-more-work.correction: The work is the same. What changes is the power, which is work divided by time.
mis.still-means-no-energy.statement: An object that is not moving has no energy.
mis.still-means-no-energy.correction: It has no kinetic energy. A book on a high shelf has a great deal of potential energy.
mis.resting-means-no-energy.statement: An object resting on something has no potential energy.
mis.resting-means-no-energy.correction: That depends entirely on how high the something is, and on where you chose to measure from.
mis.falling-loses-energy.statement: A falling object loses energy as its potential energy decreases.
mis.falling-loses-energy.correction: Its kinetic energy grows by exactly as much. The total is unchanged all the way down.
mis.law-only-for-rest.statement: The law of conservation of energy applies only to objects at rest.
mis.law-only-for-rest.correction: It applies to everything, in every situation, moving or not.
mis.friction-destroys-energy.correction: It moves it into heat and sound, which spread out too thinly to be used. Nothing is destroyed.
mis.energy-was-never-there.statement: A pendulum that stops shows the energy was never really there.
mis.energy-was-never-there.correction: It lifted the bob on every swing until it ran out, which is as real as energy gets.
mis.energy-largest-at-the-top.statement: A falling object has the most kinetic energy at the moment it is released.
mis.energy-largest-at-the-top.correction: At that moment it is still, so its kinetic energy is zero. It is largest just before it lands.
mis.energy-largest-halfway.statement: A falling object has the most kinetic energy halfway down.
mis.energy-largest-halfway.correction: Halfway down the potential and kinetic halves are equal. The kinetic half keeps growing after that.
mis.power-is-work.statement: Power and work are the same thing.
mis.power-is-work.correction: Power is work divided by the time it took. Two people can do the same work at very different powers.
mis.power-is-force.correction: Force is in newtons and power is in watts. A powerful machine does the same work sooner, not with a larger force.
mis.time-does-not-affect-power.statement: How long a job takes has no bearing on the power.
mis.time-does-not-affect-power.correctio: Time is the whole of the difference. P = W over t.
mis.parked-thing-has-energy.statement: An object standing still still has some kinetic energy, because it has mass.
mis.parked-thing-has-energy.correction: Kinetic energy is half m v squared. A velocity of zero makes the whole thing zero, however heavy the object.
mis.power-is-the-time.statement: The power of a machine is the time it takes to do a job.
mis.power-is-the-time.correction: Power is work divided by time. The time on its own is in seconds, and power is in watts.
mis.fridge-runs-constantly.statement: A fridge draws the same power all day whatever you do.
mis.fridge-runs-constantly.correction: Its compressor runs only when the inside has warmed up. Less heat getting in means fewer hours of running.
mis.standby-draws-nothing.statement: A television on standby draws no power.
mis.standby-draws-nothing.correction: It draws a few watts, and it draws them for every one of the 720 hours in a month.
mis.heater-is-cheap.statement: A room heater cannot use much energy, because it only warms the air.
mis.heater-is-cheap.correction: Heating is the most expensive thing in most houses: the power is large and the hours are long.
mis.led-uses-more.statement: A brighter lamp must be using more energy.
mis.led-uses-more.correction: Brightness and power consumption are different things. An LED gives the same light for about a sixth of the watts.
recap.s.u1.q1.ask: Name the two conditions that must both be met before work is done.
recap.s.u1.q1.answer: A force must act on the object, and the object must be displaced. Miss either one and the work is zero.
recap.s.u1.q1.listenFor: Listen for 'you have to get tired'. Tiredness is about the person and work is about the object, and keeping the two apart is the whole of this topic.
recap.s.u1.q2.ask: A coolie carries a box along a level platform at a steady walk. Explain how much work he does on the box.
recap.s.u1.q2.answer: None. The force he applies to the box is upwards, holding it, and the box travels horizontally. Work counts only displacement along the direction of the force.
recap.s.u1.q2.listenFor: Listen for 'a lot, because he walked a long way'. Distance alone is not enough: it has to be distance in the direction of the force.
recap.s.u2.q1.ask: Give the expression for work done by a constant force, and name its unit.
recap.s.u2.q1.answer: W = F s, the force multiplied by the displacement along the direction of the force. The unit is the joule, which is one newton metre.
recap.s.u2.q1.listenFor: Listen for the joule given as a unit of force. It is the unit of work and of energy, and the newton is the force.
recap.s.u2.q2.ask: A ball is thrown straight up. Describe the work gravity does on it, on the way up and on the way down.
recap.s.u2.q2.answer: Negative on the way up, because gravity opposes the motion and takes energy out of the ball. Positive on the way down, because it now acts along the motion and puts energy back in.
recap.s.u2.q2.listenFor: Listen for gravity described as always doing positive work. The sign depends on the direction of travel, not on the force.
recap.s.u3.q1.ask: Give the expression for the kinetic energy of an object.
recap.s.u3.q1.answer: Half the mass times the velocity squared, half m v squared, in joules.
recap.s.u3.q1.listenFor: Listen for mv, which is the momentum. The two are easy to mix up and they behave completely differently when the speed changes.
recap.s.u3.q2.ask: The speed of a car is doubled. Tell me what happens to its kinetic energy, and why that matters on a road.
recap.s.u3.q2.answer: It becomes four times larger, because the velocity is squared. Four times as much energy has to be taken out to stop it, which is why the stopping distance grows the way it does.
recap.s.u3.q2.listenFor: Listen for 'it doubles'. It is the natural answer and it is the reason a limit of 50 instead of 60 does more than any amount of good braking.
recap.s.u4.q1.ask: Give the expression for the potential energy of an object at a height.
recap.s.u4.q1.answer: m g h, the mass times the acceleration due to gravity times the height. It equals the work done in raising it against gravity.
recap.s.u4.q1.listenFor: Listen for mh, with the g dropped. Without it the answer is not in joules at all.
recap.s.u4.q2.ask: A crate is taken to the top of a building, once up a ladder and once up a long ramp. Explain how the work done against gravity compares.
recap.s.u4.q2.answer: It is the same both times. The work against gravity depends only on the change in height, and not at all on the path taken to get there.
recap.s.u4.q2.listenFor: Listen for 'more up the ramp, because it is further'. The ramp is longer and the force needed along it is smaller, and the two cancel exactly.
recap.s.u5.q1.ask: State the law of conservation of energy.
recap.s.u5.q1.answer: Energy can be changed from one form to another, but it cannot be created or destroyed. The total energy before and after any change is the same.
recap.s.u5.q1.listenFor: Listen for 'energy is used up'. Nothing is used up. It is moved, and often into heat, which is spread too thinly to be useful.
recap.s.u5.q2.ask: A pendulum eventually stops swinging. Explain where its energy went, and whether the law has been broken.
recap.s.u5.q2.answer: Into heat and sound, through air resistance and friction at the pivot. The law holds: add all of that up and it comes to exactly the energy the bob started with.
recap.s.u5.q2.listenFor: Listen for 'friction destroyed it'. Friction moves energy into a form nothing can use, and that is a very different claim from destroying it.
recap.s.u6.q1.ask: Define power, and give its unit.
recap.s.u6.q1.answer: Power is the rate of doing work: the work done divided by the time it took. Its unit is the watt, which is one joule per second.
recap.s.u6.q1.listenFor: Listen for power and work being treated as the same thing. Two people doing the same job in different times is the test case.
recap.s.u6.q2.ask: A bill says 250 units. Tell me what one unit is, and why bills are written that way.
recap.s.u6.q2.answer: One unit is one kilowatt hour: a kilowatt of power drawn for one hour, which comes to 3,600,000 joules. The joule is far too small to write a household bill in.
recap.s.u6.q2.listenFor: Listen for a unit described as a kilowatt. A kilowatt is a rate; a kilowatt hour is an amount, and the difference is exactly the difference between power and energy.
gloss.work: Force multiplied by the displacement along the direction of the force. Zero unless a force acts and the object moves. Measured in joules.
gloss.joule: The SI unit of work and of energy. One joule is the work done when a force of one newton moves an object one metre along its line.
gloss.energy: The capacity to do work. Measured in joules, like work, and found in several forms: mechanical, heat, chemical, electrical and light.
gloss.kinetic-energy: The energy an object has because it is moving, equal to half its mass times the square of its velocity. Doubling the speed quadruples it.
gloss.potential-energy: The energy an object has because of its position or its shape. For an object at a height it is m g h, and it equals the work done raising it.
gloss.mechanical-energy: The kinetic energy and the potential energy of an object added together. It stays constant in a free fall with no air resistance.
gloss.conservation-of-energy: Energy can be changed from one form to another but cannot be created or destroyed. The total before and after any change is the same.
gloss.conservation-of-energy.forms: law of conservation of energy|conservation of energy|conserved
gloss.power: The rate of doing work: the work done divided by the time taken. A more powerful machine does the same work sooner, not more of it.
gloss.watt: The SI unit of power, equal to one joule per second. A thousand watts is a kilowatt, which is the unit on household appliances.
gloss.kilowatt-hour: The amount of energy used by a kilowatt of power drawn for one hour, equal to 3,600,000 joules. One unit on an electricity bill.
path.guided.title: The full route
path.guided.blurb: Every topic in the order the chapter builds them.
